claims.text: Finite-temperature longitudinal spin fluctuations significantly suppress the magnetic saturation moment of fcc Fe-Co-Ni-based high-entropy alloys.
Suppression of the saturation moment by longitudinal spin fluctuations is the primary bottleneck to high magnetic energy density in these alloys.
The alloys are being considered for fusion-reactor applications.
CoCrFeMnNi is an equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
CoCrFeMnNi commonly forms a chemically disordered fcc solid solution at ambient pressure over a broad temperature range.
First-principles alloy theory can account for temperature-dependent longitudinal spin fluctuations in the paramagnetic fcc phase.
The hcp phase of CoCrFeMnNi is energetically preferable to the fcc phase at cryogenic temperatures.
Temperature-dependent longitudinal spin fluctuations are relevant to paramagnetic fcc CoCrFeMnNi from cryogenic to elevated temperatures.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations induce sizable magnetic moments on Co, Cr, and Ni atoms in CoCrFeMnNi.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations alter the net magnetic ordering of the alloy.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations affect fcc-versus-hcp phase stability.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations affect stacking-fault energy and fcc-hcp interfacial energy.
Longitudinal fluctuations reduce net saturation magnetization relative to static mean-field predictions.
CoCrFeMnNi has strong mechanical performance, including cryogenic strength, ductility, and fracture toughness.
The magnetic contribution to total energy is insufficient to stabilize fcc CoCrFeMnNi against hcp at cryogenic temperatures.
Longitudinal-spin-fluctuation effects limit the alloy's use in high-field magnetic environments.
Current state-of-the-art treatments often rely on static mean-field approximations.
Finite-temperature understanding is limited by incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically to paramagnetic fcc high-entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals.
The quantitative magnitude of longitudinal-spin-fluctuation-induced moment reduction above 77 K is unknown because suitable single-phase experimental data are lacking.
